questions.q: Why do designers establish and review 'criteria to evaluate success' when designing?
options: To increase the number of sales of a product
To ensure environmental factors are considered
To ensure the final design meets the specified needs
To maintain product awareness for further refinement of innovative products
questions.explanation: Criteria to evaluate success are the measurable functional and aesthetic benchmarks set in the proposal, used to judge objectively whether the finished project met the specified needs. This is exactly what you close the proposal-to-evaluation bookend against in H4.3.

questions.q: Outcome H4.3 requires you to do which two things when evaluating the major design project?
options: Set the criteria for success, then write the project proposal
Evaluate the project against its criteria for success, and assess the project's impact
Assess impact on the individual only, then calculate the total project cost
Test the prototype, then market the finished product to the target audience
questions.explanation: H4.3 has two halves: judge the project against the functional and aesthetic criteria set in the proposal, AND assess its impact. Students who do only one half cap the answer.

questions.q: Using the BMA (Before-Mid-After) hook, what happens at the 'Before' stage of ongoing evaluation?
options: You make the final judgement of the finished product against all the criteria
You set the criteria for success at the project proposal
You test and refine the design continually through production
You assess the impact of the project on society and the environment
questions.explanation: Before, you set the criteria at the proposal; Mid, you evaluate continually by testing and refining; After, you make the final judgement against all the criteria. The point is that evaluation is ongoing, not just a final report.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of ongoing evaluation?
options: To set goals
To explore ideas
To establish consumer needs
To solve design issues as they arise
questions.explanation: Ongoing (formative) evaluation runs throughout design and production so problems are caught and corrected early, when it is still cheap and possible to fix them. Setting goals and establishing needs happen at the start, not as part of continuous evaluation.

questions.q: When assessing the impact of the major design project using the ISE hook, which three levels do you consider?
options: Idea, Solution, Evaluation
Individual, Society, Environment
Investigation, Synthesis, Execution
Input, System, Output
questions.explanation: ISE stands for the Individual (who uses it), Society (the wider community) and the Environment, and the syllabus adds local and global, with both costs and benefits at each level. This is module two's impact skill applied to your own project.

questions.q: Why must an impact assessment weigh costs as well as benefits at each level?
options: Because NESA only awards marks for listing negative impacts
Because almost every design has both positive and negative impacts, and 'evaluate' demands a balanced judgement
Because costs are always larger than benefits for a major design project
Because the environment level has no benefits, only costs
questions.explanation: A one-sided impact ('it helps people') overstates the project's value and ignores real social and environmental costs. The verb 'evaluate' requires you to weigh both sides at the individual, society and environment levels to reach a fair, reasoned judgement.

questions.q: From memory: what two things does H4.3 require you to evaluate, and across what three levels do you assess impact?
keyPoints: Evaluate the project against its criteria for success — the functional and aesthetic criteria set in the proposal.
Assess the impact of the project.
Impact is assessed across three levels: the Individual, Society and the Environment (ISE), local and global, weighing costs and benefits.
questions.explanation: If you recalled both halves — 'against the criteria, and the impact, across individual, society and environment' — mark it Good or Easy. Missing either half is the classic trap, so grade Again or Hard.

questions.q: From memory: explain why evaluation of a major design project should be ongoing, using the Before-Mid-After structure.
keyPoints: Before: you set the criteria for success at the proposal.
Mid: you evaluate continually during design and production — testing and refining — so problems are caught early when they are still cheap to fix.
After: you make the final judgement of the finished product against all the criteria.
Ongoing evaluation keeps the project aligned with its success criteria the whole way through, rather than discovering failures too late.
questions.explanation: The BMA pattern secures the mark: catch problems early and drive refinement, describe before-during-after, and contrast with end-only evaluation.

questions.q: Why is ongoing evaluation important to a designer?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaluation gathers information so judgements can be made about a product. Ongoing evaluation keeps that information current and relevant throughout development, allowing every element of the design to be monitored continually and adjusted so that needs are met and a quality, safe product reaches the market.

criteria.descriptor: Demonstrates why ongoing evaluation is important to a designer

questions.explanation: The mark rewards linking ongoing evaluation to monitoring the design continually so problems are corrected early and the final product meets its criteria — the Before-Mid-After idea in action.

questions.q: Evaluate a major design project against its criteria for success and assess its impact on the individual, society and the environment.
questions.modelAnswer: Using a sample accessible storage unit: against its criteria for success the project largely succeeded — it met the functional criterion of supporting 100 kg, confirmed by load testing, and the criterion of tool-free assembly within 30 minutes, achieved in 25; it partly met the cost criterion, coming in slightly over budget at $160. Assessing its impact, for the individual it provides safe, accessible storage that improves daily independence, at the cost of the purchase price; for society it promotes inclusive design and could benefit many users with reduced mobility, though its production consumed resources; and for the environment, the timber and fixings have a footprint in extraction and eventual disposal, partly offset by selecting renewable, recyclable materials. Overall the project met most of its criteria and delivers a net positive impact, with a modest environmental cost.

criteria.descriptor: Evaluates the project against each named criterion with evidence, AND assesses impact at all three levels (individual, society, environment) with both costs and benefits, reaching an overall judgement.
Evaluates against criteria and describes impact across the three levels, but with limited judgement or missing costs/benefits on some levels.
Does only one half — evaluates against criteria OR assesses impact — or gives a one-sided impact.

questions.explanation: Both halves are required: judge against each measurable criterion with evidence, then weigh costs and benefits at the individual, society and environment levels, and reach an overall judgement. Doing only one half, or omitting the costs, caps the answer.
